summary: AstroGuard is a software-only health monitoring system that helps astronauts on long missions, such as a trip to Mars, notice health changes early. With communication delays of about 20 minutes to Earth, crews cannot rely on ground doctors for every decision. AstroGuard learns each astronaut's own baseline from their first 30 days of data (resting heart rate, blood oxygen, sleep and stress) and flags deviations as Watch or Critical alerts. Every alert explains what changed in plain language, for example "heart rate is 22% above your baseline and sleep fell to 4.8 hours", and suggests an action. A daily mental wellness check-in feeds the stress score, and the app generates a PDF summary for the ground medical team. It needs no wearable hardware or paid services and runs on a laptop, with optional AI-written explanations. The prototype uses simulated data and is a student prototype, not a medical device.
details:
What it does: AstroGuard tracks four daily indicators (resting heart rate, SpO2, sleep hours, stress). It builds a personal baseline (mean and standard deviation) from the first 30 days, then compares every new day against that baseline. Alerts have three levels: Normal, Watch (one metric is unusual) and Critical (several metrics deviate together, or one deviates strongly). Each alert shows actual values and percentage change, not statistics, plus a suggested action. A daily 4-question mental wellness check-in updates the stress score. A dashboard shows trends with a day selector, and a PDF report can be exported for the ground medical team.

Demo scenario: a simulated 60-day Mars mission. Days 1-30 build the baseline, Day 35 shows a small heart-rate rise (Watch), Days 45-49 show a dust storm with poor sleep, higher heart rate and stress, lower SpO2 (Critical), followed by recovery.

Why it matters: Long missions mean delayed communication with Earth, so astronauts need tools that help them understand their own health changes. Because each astronaut gets a personal baseline, the system does not depend on generic Earth ranges. Rules decide alert levels, so alerts are predictable and explainable.

Tools: Python, Flask, SQLite, pandas, NumPy, Chart.js (bundled locally), ReportLab, pytest (42 automated tests). Optional alert wording by the Google Gemini API; without internet or an API key the app uses built-in rule-based explanations. No hardware or paid services are needed.

NASA resources: we used published NASA Human Research Program material on astronaut sleep (astronauts average about 6 hours of sleep in space) as background research to motivate the project. Our demo data is simulated with generic healthy-adult values (baseline sleep around 7.3 hours) and is not derived from any NASA dataset. Because real astronaut baselines differ from Earth norms, AstroGuard builds a personal baseline for each astronaut instead of using fixed ranges.

Limitations: the data is simulated, thresholds are not clinically validated, it supports one astronaut, and it is not a medical device. Future work: radiation exposure, blood pressure, temperature, a crew view, and import of real wearable exports.
